analysis.one_liner: Adds a 10% tariff on every import, rising by 5% each year the trade deficit persists.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Ways and Means Committee with zero cosponsors until Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a new 10% tariff on every good imported into the United States, stacked on top of any existing tariffs. Each year after that, the tariff would rise by another 5% if the country ran a trade deficit in the previous year, or fall by 5% (but not below zero) if the country traded at a balance or surplus. Because the United States runs large trade deficits, the tariff would almost certainly climb well above 10% over time. It was introduced late in a two-year Congress and died in committee without a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: American producers that compete directly against imported goods, such as some manufacturers, since a broad tariff makes imports more expensive and can shift demand to domestic products. Some communities built around factory jobs could see hiring and investment if production moves back to the U.S.

how_it_helps.text: A universal 10% duty makes every imported good more expensive, which can encourage companies to produce goods in the United States and shield import-competing domestic producers from foreign competition [S2][S3].
The bill ties the tariff level to the overall trade balance, raising it 5% for each deficit year, which its sponsor presented as a way to keep pressure on until the trade deficit closes [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, who would pay higher prices on everything imported — clothing, electronics, food, household goods — with a universal tariff acting much like a broad national sales tax. American companies that depend on imported parts and materials would also face higher costs, and other countries' retaliation could hurt American exporters.

drawbacks.text: An across-the-board tariff on all imports raises prices on everyday goods for every household; economists generally find such tariffs fall hardest on lower-income families, who spend a larger share of their income on goods [S3].

Because the tariff escalates automatically every deficit year and applies to all goods with no exemptions, U.S. manufacturers that rely on imported inputs would face rising costs, and trading partners would likely respond with their own tariffs on American exports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real potential help to import-competing manufacturers and factory communities, but at the price of a large, automatic, permanently rising tax on everything American families buy. Its design is unusually blunt: it taxes all imports, even goods no American company makes, with no exemptions, and the escalation formula could push the tariff to 15%, 20% or higher as long as the overall trade deficit — which the U.S. has run for decades — persists. Most trade economists would weigh the price increases and retaliation risks against the uncertain jobs gains and call the cost too high; some industrial-policy advocates would accept it. It never advanced far enough for that argument to be tested in a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2024, referred to the Ways and Means Committee and then its Trade subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Golden, a Democrat from Maine, introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, in the final months of the 118th Congress [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tariffs, and in December it was referred to the subcommittee on Trade [S5].
No member from either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill's text would impose a 10% duty on all imports, rising 5% per deficit year and falling 5% per surplus or balanced year, never below zero, stacked on top of existing duties [S3].
The CRS summary confirms the bill directs the President to impose an additional 10% duty on all imports, adjusted annually based on the goods-and-services trade balance [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill dead, consumers and import-dependent businesses avoided the new tax on goods; the country's overall trade balance is unchanged. No one gained jobs, either — the question the bill was meant to address was never taken up.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, by default — no tariff was imposed

for.name: Rep. Jared Golden
for.role: House Representative from Maine, sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill imposing a 10% universal tariff tied to the trade balance.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member signed on from either party, so neither party took a position on the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: A universal tariff makes their foreign competitors' goods more expensive, letting them raise their own prices or take market share — but the higher prices come straight out of consumers' pockets, since the tariff applies to all imports with no exemptions.
A 10%-and-rising duty on all goods directly raises their costs on apparel, electronics, furniture and food; keeping the tariff off the books keeps shelf prices lower for shoppers too.

industries.industry: U.S. manufacturers that use imported parts and materials
industries.note: The bill taxes imports of any good, including industrial inputs, so many American factories would pay more for components even as the tariff protects them from finished-goods competition.
The bill itself does not tax exports, but a broad tariff on all goods would invite other countries to retaliate with tariffs on U.S. exports, a standard consequence of large trade barriers.
